run.question:
1. List the tables in the database and tell me the verification code from the holmes_eval_218 table
2. I'm experiencing slow queries with this SQL: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345
   Analyze why this query is slow and suggest how to fix it

report.summary: Two tables exist in schema testdb: holmes_eval_218 and orders (evidence bfb92289-fd23-4b1e-8ba2-ddf51feffda6-t0:e3357b70-d717-4477-bb55-54a27b5146ce). The verification code in holmes_eval_218 is HOLMES-MYSQL-EVAL-218-m4x9k2 (row id=1, category=eval_test) (e6b3e61b-ed7f-42fd-9713-f2320aa736ca-t0:8925a41c-a84d-483b-9afd-5574a3933dfd). For the slow-query question, the observed cause is structural: testdb.orders has only the PRIMARY index on id and no index on customer_id (e6b3e61b-ed7f-42fd-9713-f2320aa736ca-t1:f47af166-5925-4e77-9164-5e8ef2c41ae9), so EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345 plans a full Table scan on orders with a Filter on customer_id (cost=101 rows=1000, actual rows=1000 scanned, 0 rows matched) (fb135d0a-5613-47b2-867a-a0c8d4040c01-t0:e20f3c52-9f7f-4d1e-8c4e-f735015ab8f1). The table currently holds 1000 rows across 647 distinct customer_id values (fb135d0a-5613-47b2-867a-a0c8d4040c01-t1:2ff52313-7973-4c33-b450-5d3a8edcc8bf), and at that size the measured run was sub-millisecond, so the reported production slowness was not reproduced here; the full scan is the mechanism that would make the query slow as the table grows. Recommendation: create an index on orders(customer_id), then re-run EXPLAIN to confirm the plan switches from a table scan to an index lookup.

claims.text: The configured MySQL database (dialect mysql, schema testdb) contains exactly two tables: holmes_eval_218 and orders, both of type table.
holmes_eval_218 has columns id (int, PK), category (varchar(50)), verification_code (varchar(100)) and created_at (timestamp, default CURRENT_TIMESTAMP); its only index is PRIMARY on id.
The single row in holmes_eval_218 is id=1, category=eval_test, verification_code=HOLMES-MYSQL-EVAL-218-m4x9k2, read at query time 2026-11-23T18:25:20Z.

testdb.orders has columns id (int, PK), customer_id (int), order_date (date), total_amount (decimal(10,2)) and status (varchar(20)); the only index is the unique PRIMARY index on id, with no index, foreign key or unique constraint involving customer_id.

EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345 returns the plan 'Filter: (orders.customer_id = 12345) (cost=101 rows=100) (actual time=0.251..0.251 rows=0 loops=1)' over 'Table scan on orders (cost=101 rows=1000) (actual time=0.0479..0.211 rows=1000 loops=1)', i.e. every row of the table is read and filtered rather than looked up by an index.
testdb.orders currently contains 1000 rows and 647 distinct customer_id values, so the current table is small and the predicate is selective (about 1.5 rows per distinct customer_id).

On the current 1000-row dataset the query ran in about 0.25 ms actual time with 1000 rows scanned, so the reported slow-query behaviour is not reproduced by this database as read at 2026-11-23T18:25:21Z; the plan shows the mechanism (full scan) rather than an observed latency problem at this data size.

The slowness is caused by the missing index on orders.customer_id: with no usable index the optimizer can only do a full table scan plus post-filter, so cost and latency grow linearly with table size and with concurrent scans (also increasing buffer-pool/IO pressure). The reported production slowness is consistent with this plan but was not measured here.

A secondary contributor could be that SELECT * returns all columns, preventing a covering index; a composite index on (customer_id) or (customer_id, order_date/id) with an explicit column list would let the lookup and any sorting avoid the base-table reads. This is not separately observed and remains unverified.

Add a B-tree index on the filter column, e.g. CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_id ON testdb.orders (customer_id) (optionally (customer_id, order_date) if results are sorted by date), then re-run EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 12345 to confirm the plan changes to an index lookup, and re-measure latency under the real data volume; replace SELECT * with the needed columns to enable covering-index use.
